## Objectives {.unnumbered}

This lab accompanies the Week 9 notes, [*Research Software Engineering and Architecture in R*](https://soton-fds.github.io/week09.html).

- Apply a function to every element of a vector or list with `map` and its typed variants, and to several vectors in parallel with `pmap`.
- Use `walk` for functions that are called for their side effects.
- Replace a loop with `split()`, `map()` and `list_rbind()`, and check that a refactor does not change the results.
- Read many files at once, and use `possibly()` so that one failure does not stop the others.
- Write functions that check their inputs, and stop with a clear error message.

When you have finished the lab, there are more questions in `lab_09_practice.qmd`, including `map2`, `reduce`, pure functions, unit tests and Simpson's paradox.

### Task 1: From Loops to Maps

The file `data/penguins.csv` contains the penguins data from the Week 9 notes: body measurements of 344 penguins of three species, recorded on three islands in Antarctica between 2007 and 2009.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")
```

We start with two short warm-ups.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
list_of_vectors <- list(
    rnorm(20),
    rnorm(20, mean = 1),
    rnorm(20, mean = -1, sd = 2)
)
numbers <- 1:10
summary_stats <- list(mean, median, sd, var)
```

- [x] Calculate the mean of each vector in `list_of_vectors`.
- [x] For each statistic in `summary_stats`, apply the statistic to `numbers`.

::: {.solution}
```{r}
map_dbl(list_of_vectors, \(v) mean(v))
map_dbl(summary_stats, \(v) v(numbers))
```
:::

Next we use `pmap` to draw several plots of the penguins at once.

```{r}
variables <- c("flipper_length_mm", "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm")
```

- [x] For each `<variable>` in `variables`, produce a plot of that variable against `body_mass_g` in `penguins`. (*Hint*: each `<variable>` is a string, not a column; recall `.data[[...]]` from Lab 8.)
- [x] Create a vector of display names for the $y$-axes and add them to your plot.
- [x] Create a vector of titles and add them to your plot.

::: {.solution}
```{r}
display_names = c("flipper length (mm)", "bill length (mm)", "bill depth (mm)")
title <- c("flipper length against body mass", "bill length against body mass", "bill depth against body mass")
pmap(list(variables, display_names, title) , \(a, b, c) ggplot(penguins, aes( x = body_mass_g , y = .data[[a]])) + geom_point() + labs( x = "body mass (g)" , y = b, title = c))
```
:::

Finally, we replace a loop with `map`.
The code below uses a `for` loop to fit a separate straight line of bill depth against bill length for each species of penguin, and collects the slopes and intercepts into a tibble.
(`lm()` fits the line, and `coef()` extracts its intercept and slope.)

- [ ] Rewrite the code using `purrr` instead of a loop. (*Hint*: see *Working with Lists of Results* in the [Week 9 notes](https://soton-fds.github.io/week09.html), and look up `split()` and `list_rbind()`.)

```{r}
species <- unique(penguins$species)
results <- list()

for (sp in species) {
    data <- penguins |> filter(species == sp)

    # fit a linear regression model of bill depth vs. bill length
    model <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = data)

    # Extract the slope and intercept
    slope <- coef(model)["bill_length_mm"]
    intercept <- coef(model)["(Intercept)"]

    # Store the results
    results[[sp]] <- tibble(
        species = sp,
        slope = slope,
        intercept = intercept
    )
}

# put into a data frame
loop_results <- bind_rows(results)
loop_results
```

::: {.solution}
```{r}
species_tibbles <- split(penguins, penguins$species)

regres_function <- function(data) {
  model <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = data)
  slope <- coef(model)["bill_length_mm"]
  intercept <- coef(model)["(Intercept)"]
  results = tibble(
        slope = slope,
        intercept = intercept)
}
results <- map(species_tibbles, \(v) regres_function(v))
linear_regression_table <- list_rbind(results, names_to = "species")
linear_regression_table

```
:::

- [x] A refactor should change how the code is organised, without changing what it does. Check that your version gives the same results as the loop. If it doesn't, why not?

::: {.solution}
The new code gives the same outcome just with two of the columns in different order. 
:::

### Task 2: Many Files, and Failing Well

Research data often arrive as many files with the same format, such as one file per site or per field season.
The folder `data/penguins` contains the penguins data as one CSV file per species per year.

- [x] Read all of the CSV files in `data/penguins` into a single tibble, with a column recording which file each row came from. Look at what is in the folder first. (*Hint*: see *Working with Lists of Results* in the [Week 9 notes](https://soton-fds.github.io/week09.html); `set_names()` will help you keep track of which file is which.)

::: {.solution}
```{r}
#| message: FALSE
files = list.files("data/penguins", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
species_per_year = files |> set_names() |> map(read_csv)      # a list of tibbles, one per file
all_penguins_data = species_per_year |> list_rbind(names_to = "species")
all_penguins_data
```
:::

- [x] Use `fit_bill_model()` from Task 1 to fit a separate line of bill depth against bill length for each file. Your code should fail. Which file causes the problem, and why?

::: {.solution}
```{r}
#| error: TRUE
all_lines <- species_per_year |> map(regres_function())
all_lines_table <- map(all_lines, \(v) list_rbind(v))
all_lines_table

```
:::

- [x] Change your code so that a file that cannot be fitted no longer stops the others. Check which files failed, and combine the results for the others into a single tibble.

::: {.solution}
```{r}
#| error: TRUE
sensible_lin_regres <- possibly(regres_function, otherwise = NULL)
sensible_all_lines_table <- map(species_per_year, \(v) sensible_lin_regres(v)) |> list_rbind()
sensible_all_lines_table
```
:::

- [x] Is it reasonable simply to leave out the file that failed? What would you report alongside these results?

::: {.solution}
It is not reasonable to leave out an entire data set as this may hide important results. I would report that one of the data sets was left out as there were not recorded data in that data set. 
:::

The error from `lm()` above, `0 (non-NA) cases`, comes from deep inside `lm()`, and doesn't say much about what is actually wrong with the data.

- [x] Change `fit_bill_model()` so that it checks its input first, and stops with a clear error message if there are fewer than two penguins with both bill measurements. Why two?

::: {.solution}
```{r}
regres_function <- function(data) {
  clean_data <- data |> filter(is.na(bill_length_mm) == FALSE) |> filter(is.na(bill_depth_mm)== FALSE)
  if(length(clean_data) < 2){
    stop("Need more than 2 penguins with both measurements in data frame")
   }
  
  model <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = data)
  slope <- coef(model)["bill_length_mm"]
  intercept <- coef(model)["(Intercept)"]
  results = tibble(
        slope = slope,
        intercept = intercept)
}


regres_function(all_penguins_data)
```
:::
